question: According to the Ghanaian Constitution, where does the Sovereignty of Ghana reside?
ground_truth: The Sovereignty of Ghana resides in the people of Ghana in whose name and for whose welfare the powers of government are to be exercised in the manner and within the limits laid down in the Constitution.

question: What is the age threshold for defining a child according to Article 28 of the Ghanaian Constitution?
ground_truth: A child means a person below the age of eighteen years.

question: What does freedom of movement in Ghana include according to Article 21?
ground_truth: Freedom of movement means the right to move freely in Ghana, the right to leave and to enter Ghana, and immunity from expulsion from Ghana.

question: Under what circumstances may a person not be held to have deprived another person of their life according to Article 13 of the Ghanaian Constitution?
ground_truth: A person shall not be held to have deprived another person of their life if that other person dies as a result of a lawful act of war or if that other person dies as a result of the use of force to such an extent as is reasonably justifiable in the particular circumstances, including: (a) defence of any person from violence or defence of property; (b) effecting a lawful arrest or preventing the escape of a person lawfully detained; (c) suppressing a riot, insurrection or mutiny; or (d) preventing the commission of a crime by that person.

question: What are the exceptions to forced labour according to Article 16 of the Ghanaian Constitution?
ground_truth: The exceptions to forced labour include: (a) any labour required as a result of a sentence or order of a court; (b) any labour required of a member of a disciplined force or service as his duties or, in the case of a person with conscientious objections to Armed Forces service, labour required by law in place of such service; (c) any labour required during war, emergency or calamity that threatens the life and well-being of the community, to the extent reasonably justifiable; and (d) any labour reasonably required as part of normal communal or other civic obligations.

question: What conditions must be satisfied before the State can compulsorily take possession of or acquire any property?
ground_truth: The State must satisfy two conditions: (a) the taking of possession or acquisition must be necessary in the interest of defence, public safety, public order, public morality, public health, town and country planning or the development or utilization of property in a manner that promotes public benefit; and (b) the necessity for the acquisition must be clearly stated and provide reasonable justification for any hardship caused to persons with an interest in or right over the property.

question: What rights do persons aggrieved by administrative acts and decisions have according to the constitution?
ground_truth: Persons aggrieved by the exercise of such acts and decisions have the right to seek redress before a court or other tribunal.

question: What three conditions must be met when discretionary power is vested in any person or authority according to the Constitution?
ground_truth: According to the Constitution, discretionary power must: (a) imply a duty to be fair and candid; (b) not be arbitrary, capricious or biased by resentment, prejudice or personal dislike and shall be in accordance with due process of law; and (c) be governed by regulations published by constitutional or statutory instrument if the person or authority is not a judge or other judicial officer.

question: What are the two ways a treaty, agreement or convention executed by the President can be ratified according to Article 75?
ground_truth: A treaty, agreement or convention can be ratified by (a) Act of Parliament or (b) a resolution of Parliament supported by the votes of more than one-half of all the members of Parliament.

question: What must accompany a bill when it is introduced in Parliament according to Article 106?
ground_truth: A bill must be accompanied by an explanatory memorandum setting out in detail the policy and principles of the bill, the defects of the existing law, the remedies proposed to deal with those defects and the necessity for its introduction. Additionally, it must be published in the Gazette at least fourteen days before the date of its introduction in Parliament.

question: What is the voting requirement for matters in Parliament according to the Constitution?
ground_truth: Matters in Parliament shall be determined by the votes of the majority of members present and voting, with at least half of all the members of Parliament present.

question: What constitutes a quorum of Parliament apart from the person presiding?
ground_truth: A quorum of Parliament, apart from the person presiding, shall be one-third of all the members of Parliament.

question: What is the timeframe within which the Council of State must complete consideration of a bill under normal circumstances?
ground_truth: The Council of State shall complete consideration of a bill within thirty days after the third reading in Parliament of that bill, except where the bill was passed under a certificate of urgency, in which case it shall be considered and reported within seventy-two hours.

question: What is the composition of the Cabinet according to the Constitution?
ground_truth: The Cabinet shall consist of the President, the Vice-President and not less than ten and not more than nineteen Ministers of State.

question: What is the maximum number of terms a person can be elected to hold office as President of Ghana?
ground_truth: A person shall not be elected to hold office as President of Ghana for more than two terms.

question: What is the maximum time period within which another presidential election must be held if three or more candidates obtain the two highest numbers of votes?
ground_truth: Another election shall be held within twenty-one days after the previous election.

question: How often must the Electoral Commission review the division of Ghana into constituencies?
ground_truth: The Electoral Commission shall review the division of Ghana into constituencies at intervals of not less than seven years, or within twelve months after the publication of the enumeration figures after the holding of a census of the population of Ghana, whichever is earlier.

question: What conditions must a prospective political party satisfy for registration according to Article 55(7)?
ground_truth: A prospective political party must furnish the electoral commission with a copy of its constitution and the names and addresses of its national officers, and must satisfy that: (a) there is ordinarily residence, or registered as a voter in each district of Ghana, at least one founding member of the party; (b) the party has branches in all the regions of Ghana and is organized in not less than two thirds of the districts of each region; and (c) the party's name, emblem, colour, motto or any other symbol has no ethnic, regional, religious or other sectional connotations or gives the appearance that its activities are confined only to a part of Ghana.

question: How often are elections to the District Assemblies held?
ground_truth: Elections to the District Assemblies shall be held every four years, except that such elections and elections to Parliament shall be held at least six months apart.

question: What jurisdiction does the High Court have regarding Parliament members and the Speaker?
ground_truth: The High Court has jurisdiction to hear and determine questions about whether a person has been validly elected as a member of Parliament or if a member's seat has become vacant, and whether a person has been validly elected as Speaker of Parliament or has vacated the office of Speaker.

question: What is the exclusive jurisdiction of the Supreme Court regarding official documents?
ground_truth: The Supreme Court has exclusive jurisdiction to determine whether an official document shall not be produced in court because its production or the disclosure of its contents will be prejudicial to the security of the State or will be injurious to the public interest.

question: What are the minimum qualifications required for appointment as a Justice of the High Court?
ground_truth: A person must be of high moral character and proven integrity and must have at least ten years' standing as a lawyer.

question: Under what conditions can the President suspend the Chief Justice according to Article 146?
ground_truth: The President may suspend the Chief Justice in the case where a petition has been referred to a committee, and the President must act in accordance with the advice of the Council of State and by warrant signed by him.

question: Who has the authority to remove a panel member of a Regional Tribunal other than the Chairman?
ground_truth: The Chief Justice acting on the advice of the Judicial Council and of the Regional Co-ordinating Council.

question: How is revenue from stool lands distributed according to Article 267?
ground_truth: Revenue from stool lands is distributed as follows: twenty-five percent to the stool through the traditional authority for maintenance of the stool in keeping with its status, twenty percent to the traditional authority, and fifty-five percent to the District Assembly within the area of authority of which the stool lands are situated.

question: What happens to a freehold interest in land in Ghana held by a non-citizen on August 22, 1969?
ground_truth: It shall be deemed to be a leasehold interest for a period of fifty years at a peppercorn rent commencing from August 22, 1969, and the freehold reversionary interest shall vest in the President on behalf of, and in trust for, the people of Ghana.

question: What are the three main functions of the Judicial Council as outlined in the constitution?
ground_truth: The three main functions of the Judicial Council are: (a) to propose judicial reforms to improve the level of administration of justice and efficiency in the Judiciary; (b) to be a forum for consideration and discussion of matters relating to the discharge of the functions of the Judiciary and assist the Chief Justice in ensuring efficiency and effective realization of justice; and (c) to perform any other functions conferred on it by or under the Constitution or any other law not inconsistent with the Constitution.

question: What are the main functions of the National House of Chiefs according to the Constitution?
ground_truth: The National House of Chiefs shall: (a) advise any person or authority charged with any responsibility under the Constitution or any other law for any matter relating to or affecting chieftaincy; (b) undertake the progressive study, interpretation and codification of customary law with a view to evolving a unified system of rules of customary law, and compiling the customary laws and lines of succession applicable to each stool or skin; (c) undertake an evaluation of traditional customs and usages with a view to eliminating those that are outmoded and socially harmful; and (d) perform such other functions not inconsistent with any function assigned to the House of Chiefs of a region, as Parliament may refer to it.

question: What powers does a commission of inquiry have in respect of examining witnesses?
ground_truth: A commission of inquiry has the powers, rights and privileges of the High Court or a Justice of the High Court at a trial, including the power to enforce the attendance of witnesses and examine them on oath, affirmation or otherwise.

question: What happens to public corporations that existed before the coming into force of the Constitution until Parliament enacts a new Act?
ground_truth: Until Parliament enacts an Act of Parliament in accordance with article 192 of the Constitution for the establishment or operation of a public corporation, a public corporation in existence immediately before the coming into force of the Constitution shall continue its operations under the enactment under which it was established.

question: What is the official retirement age for active-duty officers in the Ghana Armed Forces?
ground_truth: The official retirement age for active-duty officers in the Ghana Armed Forces is sixty years. This is stated generally for public officers, including those in the public service such as the Armed Forces, who shall retire on attaining the age of sixty years unless otherwise provided by the Constitution (Article 199, p.145).
